doc.title: Dave Liebman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Audience reaction to late Coltrane; Tyner and Elvin leave
summary: They wonder how Coltrane felt about audiences walking out in 1965-66 and why Tyner and Elvin Jones left.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Isn’t it – when you think about it though, especially then, where he played, from ’65 until the end, he must have been aware of the – not antipathy, but of the reaction. I remember Newport, seeing him in ’66, the people – and the Titans of the Tenor Saxophone story. I always tell that story. Half the audience left Lincoln Center. He must have known that. He didn’t have his eyes closed. This is a big difference in the response from – you hear the Europe concerts in ’63. They’re playing Mr. PC then. They’re playing Impressions. The people are enthusiastic. Then you hear this. Is this because it was America, where you just don’t know anything? Or it’s just because he was really taking it far out? He must have felt that vibe. How could he not? I think about that.

I get the impression from reading stuff that he said in interviews and whatever that he just felt that it was what he had to do, regardless of the consequences. He just felt that that was the course he had to take.

But imagine the guys getting off the bandstand. You know how you are, when you’re on with your guys, and you get off the bandstand. “Man, it was weird out there.” Somebody’s thinking something. There’s four guys up there. Maybe nobody’s talking about it, but you got to think, God, they just got up in the middle and left. What a drag.
For example, at the end of ’65 McCoy Tyner and Elvin Jones left, because they couldn’t deal with the way the music was going. Did you ever talk to Elvin about this? Did he ever say anything?

No. It’s just what I read, what you read, that it was too loud, two drummers, and I think ego-wise, he didn’t want to be competing with anybody else. You know the way he was. And Rashied [Ali], he was the kid on the block. Who knows? McCoy couldn’t hear himself, he says.
But Elvin never said anything to you about this?
No. I would think that would be taboo.
